content:
Honestly? No, it wasn't fair.

From a pure intergenerational equity standpoint, asking a 22-year-old apprentice to fund additional pension benefits for 71-year-olds through taxes and contributions—especially when that young person is still in the early training phase of their career—creates an imbalance where today’s retirees are receiving significant financial support that has to be paid for by the next generation still building their own financial foundation.

That younger generation will not only bear the cost today but may also face reduced pension prospects or higher contribution rates in their own future retirements as a result of this policy. If fairness means both generations should experience a reasonably proportionate distribution of economic burden and benefit, then prioritizing an immediate benefit for retirees at the direct expense of those entering the workforce or just establishing themselves seems structurally unfair to the young.

It also sends a message that current retirees’ comfort takes precedence over the economic stability of those just beginning their adult earning years—something that can strain family dynamics and societal solidarity if younger generations feel they're being asked to subsidize an entitlement they will likely never fully access in the same form when their time comes.
